source.title_on_document: Deepening ideas vs. exploring new ones: AI strategy effects in human-AI creative collaboration

supplement.where: PLOS One Supporting information listed on p. 23: S1 File (DOCX), S2 File (DOCX), S3 File (XLSX). The document prints no URL for them beyond the article DOI, https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0340449.
supplement.holds: S1: prompt templates for the Vertical and Horizontal strategies and the API settings (GPT-4.1, temperature 0.0, max_tokens 400, n = 1, JSON output). S2: interface instructions with video explanations, experimental materials, and the complete questionnaire items (GQS, MDMT). S3: the complete dataset. The descriptions list no result tables. Every statistic recorded here is printed in the main text (Tables 1-7, Figs 6 and 8).

paper_design_summary: Japanese crowd workers on Yahoo! Crowdsourcing (165 recruited, 148 analyzed after those who experienced GPT API errors were excluded) each did one 15-minute brainstorming session on 'How to increase sales for a city cafe', taking turns with GPT-4.1 to place ideas on a shared 15x15 grid (20 ideas each). They were divided, by a method the paper does not state, into three between-participants arms that differ only in the AI's strategy: Vertical (deepens existing ideas, 52 analyzed), Horizontal (opens new topics, 50 analyzed), or Random (the AI picks either strategy at random, the paper's control, 46 analyzed). The outcomes are counts of the session ideas each participant would 'actually want to adopt', trust (MDMT) and Godspeed questionnaires, and a t-SNE plot of idea embeddings, with no rater or computed creativity or diversity score of the output.

studies.label: Turn-based human-AI brainstorming with three AI strategies (Vertical, Horizontal, Random)

assignment.what_was_assigned: The AI partner's strategy: Vertical (deepening), Horizontal (broadening), or Random (the AI picks between the two at random). All arms work with GPT-4.1, and no arm works without AI. The paper does not describe how participants were allocated to conditions.
assignment.quote: We divided 148 participants into three groups: a deepening strategy (vertical), a diffusion strategy (horizontal), and a random control condition.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Introduction; p. 10, Study design and conditions ('This study conducted a one-factor, three-level between-participants experiment.'). No sentence states how participants were allocated; 'random' in the Random condition (p. 11) refers to the AI's choice of strategy.

arms.name: Vertical (Deepening)
arms.description: GPT-4.1 deepens an existing idea by adding a related idea in the same column, taking the leftmost column with fewer than nine ideas (Algorithm 1, p. 9).

arms.name: Horizontal (Broadening)
arms.description: GPT-4.1 places ideas in new or sparsely filled columns from a completely new direction; an idea placed in row 1 or later derives from the row-0 idea of its column (Algorithm 2, p. 10).

arms.name: Random (Control)
arms.description: The AI randomly selects between the Vertical and Horizontal strategies. The paper calls this arm 'A control group'.

participants.exclusions: 165 participants were recruited on May 24-25, 2025. Those who experienced GPT API errors were excluded, leaving 148 in the final analysis (17 fewer, by subtraction). The paper gives no exclusions by condition and no count at assignment; 165 is a recruitment count.
participants.who: Yahoo! Crowdsourcing workers paid 70 JPY each. Of the 148 analyzed, 115 were male (77.7%), 32 female (21.6%), and one other (0.7%), with a mean age of 47.93 (SD 10.56, median 49.0). No prior survey of AI proficiency or creative-task experience was run.
participants.country: Japan (p. 22: 'the study was conducted only with Japanese participants')
participants.quote: we recruited 165 participants between May 24,2025 and May 25, 2025 via Yahoo! Crowdsourcing, with a compensation of 70 JPY each. After excluding those who experienced GPT API errors, 148 participants were included in the final analysis.
participants.locator: p. 11, Study design and conditions; p. 11, Table 1 (Horizontal 50, Vertical 52, Random 46, Total 148); p. 22, Limitations

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4.1 via the OpenAI API (temperature 0.0, max_tokens 400, n = 1, JSON response format)
ai_tool.how_used: Strict turn-taking co-ideation partner: the participant and the AI alternately place one idea on a shared 15x15 grid, 20 ideas each and up to 40 per session (p. 8). The AI's prompt asks for an idea of about 15 characters (pp. 9-10). The paper states no length limit for participants' ideas. The system prompts the AI with the session theme and the content and position of all existing ideas, and the AI places its idea where the arm's strategy dictates (Algorithms 1 and 2, pp. 9-10). The paper describes no chat with the AI. The nearest listed role is ideas_supplied.

task.description: Brainstorm ideas on 'How to increase sales for a city cafe' with the AI on the grid; then, in an evaluation phase shown without the grid layout, select from all session ideas (human and AI) those the participant would 'actually want to adopt'; then a post-session questionnaire.
task.duration: 15-minute main session (p. 11), after a briefing with video instructions and a practice session

outcomes.name: Number of AI-generated ideas the participant selected for adoption
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: After the session each participant picks, from all ideas of their own session shown without the grid layout, the ideas they would 'actually want to adopt' (p. 11). The outcome counts the picked ideas that the AI generated. It is a choice recorded in the evaluation interface, an adoption intention rather than an adoption, and not a creativity rating by raters or a computed score: the authors say whether selected ideas are truly creative 'requires separate evaluation' (p. 20). Kruskal-Wallis test across the three arms with post-hoc pairwise tests (method not named).

outcomes.name: Probability that an idea is selected (idea-level mixed-effects logistic regression, strategy terms)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Binary selection of each idea (human and AI ideas, all three arms) regressed on AI condition, creator (AI vs human), standardized grid row and column, content length, and five embedding-similarity metrics, with a participant (sessionId) random effect; AUC = 0.799 (p. 16). Pairwise strategy comparisons come from emmeans (Table 7). The Table 7 note says the strategy differences are under 3 percentage points in predicted probabilities, and the Conclusion cites a '2.36 percentage point improvement for the Vertical strategy over Random' (p. 23); no table prints these probabilities.

contrasts.reported: Vertical vs. Random: OR 1.13, 95% CI 0.658-1.95, p = 0.658 (N = 5,848 ideas from 148 participants)
Horizontal vs. Random: OR 1.04, 95% CI 0.600-1.81, p = 0.882
Vertical vs. Horizontal: OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.626-1.89, p = 0.765

outcomes.name: Dispersion of ideas in a t-SNE map of idea embeddings, by AI strategy
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Each idea is converted to an embedding with unnamed 'text embedding models' (p. 12) and projected to two dimensions with t-SNE. Fig 8A colors the Vertical (n=2071 ideas) and Horizontal (n=1942 ideas) pools; the Random arm is not shown. The comparison is visual: Vertical ideas 'appear in relatively dense clusters' and Horizontal ideas are 'more widely dispersed' (p. 15). Each pool mixes human and AI ideas (Fig 8B: Human n = 1973, AI n = 2040), so the plot does not isolate participants' own outputs. The Discussion adds that ideas 'generated under different AI strategies occupy different regions in the semantic space' (p. 19). The field scored_on_output is true only because the map is computed from the ideas' embeddings. The paper reports no dispersion or similarity number by arm, so this outcome does not meet criterion 3 (see eligibility.reason).

contrasts.reported: Fig 8 panel A legend: Horizontal (n=1942), Vertical (n=2071) ideas. Text: 'ideas from the vertical condition appear in relatively dense clusters while ideas from the horizontal condition are more widely dispersed across the latent space.' No metric, interval, or test.
contrasts.locator: p. 15, t-SNE visualization of the latent space; p. 16, Fig 8 panel A; p. 19, RQ3 ('distinct strategy-based clustering patterns')

diversity_detail.metric: Visual dispersion of each condition's ideas on a 2-D t-SNE map; no numeric diversity metric
diversity_detail.computed_over: All ideas (human and AI) pooled across sessions within each of the Vertical and Horizontal arms, projected jointly
diversity_detail.uncertainty: None; no statistic, interval, or test
diversity_detail.notes: Direction is coded on dispersion (higher means more diverse), so no sign reversal: Vertical, the treatment, is less dispersed. Counts are ideas, not people. The AI's prompts set how each AI idea relates to existing ideas (pp. 9-10), and the plot does not separate human ideas by condition. The per-idea similarity metrics (theme similarity; average, maximum, minimum, and SD of similarity to other ideas in the same session) enter only as predictors of selection (Table 5) and are never compared across arms.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 3 is not met. No creativity or diversity score of the output, by raters or by a computed measure, is compared across arms. The outcomes are counts of ideas each participant would 'actually want to adopt' and their idea-level logit (the participant's own choice, whose creativity the authors say 'requires separate evaluation', p. 20), trust and Godspeed questionnaires, and perception of the AI's strategy. The only diversity evidence is a t-SNE plot with no metric or test. It pools participants' ideas with the AI's ideas, which follow each arm's prompt (pp. 9-10), and it omits the Random arm (Fig 8A, p. 16). Criterion 1 is unclear: all three arms use GPT-4.1 and differ only in strategy (an ai_design comparison), but the paper says only that participants were 'divided' into three groups (p. 3) and never states random allocation. 'Random' names an AI condition. S1 is therefore coded design_class other, as in the final c168. Random allocation would make it an online_rct and meet criterion 1, and the paper would still fail criterion 3. Criterion 2 is met: 148 people analyzed of 165 recruited (52, 50, and 46; Table 1, p. 11), well above 50. Context class is none: there is no AI-free arm, and the paper studies how people trust and adopt AI-made ideas, which the codebook lists in the screening report and omits from the dataset.

one_line_finding: With GPT-4.1 as a turn-taking brainstorming partner in every arm, participants whose AI deepened existing ideas (Vertical) selected more AI ideas to adopt than those whose AI broadened (Horizontal), 6.98 vs 5.22 (three-arm Kruskal-Wallis H(2) = 6.71, p = 0.035; post-hoc p = 0.037; Table 4, p. 14), and reported higher competence trust (4.79 vs 4.04 Horizontal and 4.16 Random; F(2,145) = 5.07, p = 0.007; Table 2, p. 13), while total ideas selected did not differ (H = 3.55, p = 0.169; Table 4) and no creativity or diversity score of the output was reported.
open_questions: How were participants allocated to the three conditions? The paper says only 'We divided 148 participants into three groups' (p. 3) and never states random assignment, so S1 is coded design_class other. Random allocation would make S1 an online_rct and meet criterion 1, but criterion 3 would still fail.
How were the 17 participants excluded for GPT API errors (165 recruited, 148 analyzed) spread across the arms? The paper gives no per-arm exclusions.
Does the S3 dataset hold the idea texts with creator and condition? If so, a computed diversity measure of participants' own ideas across arms could be built, though the paper reports none.
notes: Outcomes compared across arms but not listed, because they are questionnaires rather than scores of the output: perception of the AI's strategy (chi2(4, N = 148) = 23.09, p = .0001, Cramer's V = .279; 'unclear' 7.7% Vertical, 28.0% Horizontal, 23.9% Random; p. 13), MDMT trust (Table 2, p. 13: Competence Trust Vertical 4.79 (1.11), Horizontal 4.04 (1.42), Random 4.16 (1.26), F(2,145) = 5.07, p = 0.007, eta^2 = 0.065; Moral Trust F(2,145) = 4.12, p = 0.018, eta^2 = 0.054), and Godspeed scales (Table 3, p. 14; only Perceived Safety reaches F(2,145) = 3.06, p = 0.050). Also not listed: Fig 8 panel B, which contrasts human ideas (n = 1973) with AI ideas (n = 2040) from the same assisted sessions and answers none of the three questions; the grid heatmaps (Fig 7); and the per-idea similarity metrics, used only as predictors of selection (Table 5). Both Fig 8 panels total 4,013 ideas, against 5,848 ideas from 148 sessions in the selection analyses (pp. 13, 16). Fig 6 (p. 15) labels each panel with p and eta^2: AI 0.035* and 0.032, user (human) 0.179 and 0.010, total 0.169 and 0.011. Inconsistencies in the PDF: the average-similarity OR is 1.37 in the p. 16 text, 1.35 in Table 5 (p. 17) and on pp. 19-20, and 1.33 on pp. 20, 21, and 23; the grid-row OR is 0.716 in the p. 16 text and 0.719 in Table 5 and on pp. 19 and 22; the content-length OR is 1.17 in the p. 16 text and 1.15 in Table 5; eta^2 for AI ideas selected is 0.033 in the text (p. 13) and 0.032 on Fig 6; the Vertical gain over Horizontal in AI ideas selected is '34%' on pp. 18, 21, and 22 and '35%' on p. 21; the Conclusion's '2.36 percentage point improvement for the Vertical strategy over Random' (p. 23) comes from a predictive probability analysis that no table reports. Page numbers are the printed page numbers, which match the PDF page indices (1/26 to 26/26). Reconciled from forms A and B against the full markdown and PDF pp. 1-3 and 7-23, with Fig 6 and Fig 8 read from high-resolution renders. This file replaces a reconciliation of October 4, 2026 built from earlier raw forms; that version coded design_class other, ai_tool.role ideas_supplied, the selection outcomes as self_report, and S1-O5 as secondary. Final check, 2026-10-05: no challenge files exist for c078. The checkers run only on forms reconciled as core yes or unclear, and this form was reconciled as core no. No checker problem was resolved, so final.challenge_resolution is empty. The finalizer checked the form against the PDF instead: the page images of pp. 1-3 and 6-23, the text layer of pp. 1-23, and the full markdown with its reference list. Every number in the reported strings, the notes, and one_line_finding matches its cited page. The Fig 6 panel labels and the Fig 8 legends were read again from high-resolution renders. The two reconciler additions marked confirmed false in reconciliation.agreed_fields_checked match the PDF: the S1-O2 Vertical vs Horizontal contrast (Table 4 and its note, p. 14) and the Fig 6 labels (p. 15). A search of the text layer of pp. 1-23 for random, assign, allocat, counterbalanc, divided, batch, and registration terms finds no statement of how participants were allocated. The finalizer made five edits. (1) studies[S1].design_class is now other, not online_rct. The codebook reserves online_rct for randomized experiments, the paper never states random allocation, and the final c168 codes the same situation as other. The reconciliation says that c168 keeps online_rct, which does not hold, and the c054 assignment checker refuted online_rct on the same ground. (2) paper_design_summary gives the 165 recruited and says 'analyzed' for the 148 and for each arm, and participants.who ties the gender and age figures to the 148 analyzed. (3) ai_tool.how_used attributes the 'about 15 characters' limit to the AI's prompt only (pp. 9-10), because the paper states no length limit for participants' ideas. (4) S1-O5 cites the p. 19 statement that ideas under different strategies 'occupy different regions in the semantic space', and its measure_detail says why scored_on_output true does not meet criterion 3. (5) Open question 1 and eligibility.reason follow the design-class change, and eligibility.reason adds that the AI half of the t-SNE pool follows each arm's prompt. The criteria and core are unchanged. The reconciliation object is unchanged, so its agreed field for design_class keeps online_rct. On p. 6 the ethics approval number breaks across a line ('R5-' then '20-2'), so the reconciliation's 'R520-2' may be 'R5-20-2'.

open_items.item: Allocation to the three arms (open question 1): the paper says only 'We divided 148 participants into three groups' (p. 3) and calls the study a 'one-factor, three-level between-participants experiment' (p. 10). No sentence in pp. 1-23 says how participants were allocated, and 'Random' names the arm in which the AI picks a strategy at random (p. 11). Random allocation would make S1 an online_rct and meet criterion 1. It cannot make the paper core, because criterion 3 is not met. The supplement descriptions (p. 23) do not mention allocation.

Exclusions by arm (open question 2): 165 were recruited and 148 analyzed after those who experienced GPT API errors were excluded (17 fewer, by subtraction). The paper gives no count at assignment and no split by arm. Criterion 2 rests on the 148 analyzed (52, 50, and 46; Table 1, p. 11) and holds under any split. The split bears on n_randomized and on differential exclusion, not on eligibility.

Contents of the S3 dataset (open question 3): whether it holds each idea's text with its creator and condition. Criterion 3 asks for a creativity or diversity score of the output, and the paper reports none, so S3 does not change eligibility under the codebook as written. It would matter only if Review 1 decided to compute a diversity measure of participants' own ideas from posted data.
